dimensions.gloss: Which technical identity, configuration, and provenance details of the AI model or tool are recorded, such as its name, version, vendor, parameters, and archiving.
dimensions.note: Minimum attributable fields (law_regulation: Model ID, Prompts, Human Contribution, Timestamp, Signature) is a close call — it lists required attribution fields rather than model metadata per se, but the fields overlap heavily with the model-identity items above.

dimensions.gloss: How much of the output the AI produced relative to the human, expressed as an ordered level, a percentage, a macro/micro split, or an authorship pattern.
dimensions.note: Locus of responding, nature of ai output, and patterns are close calls: each names a different framework (an instructional-arrangement typology, a submission-originality check, a message-generation typology) but all measure the same underlying human-vs-AI share of the output.

dimensions.gloss: Whether AI use is permitted, prohibited, or restricted to specific tasks, and how broadly that permission extends.
dimensions.note: 'Policy' (values Disclosure/Prohibition) and 'no-delegate zones' are close calls — they express the same allow/forbid axis through a binary policy field and a named exclusion zone respectively, rather than a permission list.

dimensions.gloss: Whether and how reviewers or editors are allowed to use AI tools during peer review.
variants: policies governing reviewer and editor use of ai

dimensions.gloss: Where in the document, submission, or workflow the disclosure statement is expected to appear.

dimensions.canonical_label: Scientific domain of the AI use-case
dimensions.gloss: Which scientific or research subject-matter domain the example AI use-case belongs to.
dimensions.note: These four all come from one quote enumerating use-case categories; each was extracted as its own label though they are values of a single 'domain' axis.

dimensions.gloss: Whether disclosing or labelling AI use is required, recommended, or optional, who bears that obligation, and how strongly it is stated.
dimensions.note: Policy status (does any policy/statement exist at all) and policy strength (require/recommend/accept/none) are close calls next to the flat mandatory-disclosure yes/no fields, but all describe the same underlying obligation axis at different granularities.

dimensions.gloss: What license or copyright terms apply to the disclosed item, entry, or repository.
variants: license and copyright information, both for individual entries and for the registry or repository as a whole

dimensions.gloss: Whether publishing the calculation methodology behind a health-technology assessment figure (budget impact, health gain, cost) is mandatory, recommended, or not required.
variants: methodology of calculating the health gain by the new technology
dimensions.note: Three checklist items from what appears to be one HTA scheme, each applying the identical mandatory/recommended/none scale to a different calculation subject.

dimensions.gloss: How specific or detailed the prescribed disclosure/provenance mechanism and its requirements are, ranging from broad or example-based to exhaustive.
dimensions.note: P4 and P5 are two distinct coding items in their source scheme (the mechanism itself vs. requirements imposed on it), but both track the same broad-to-specific axis as 'mechanism presentation', so they were merged.

dimensions.gloss: How the AI's output or performance was evaluated after the fact, including methods, metrics, and output variability/reproducibility.
Whether a generative AI tool can be credited as an author or co-author.
variants: no authorship is allowed for generative artificial intelligence
policy on ai tool as an author

dimensions.gloss: What kind of task or contribution the AI performed, such as editing, drafting, analysis, or information retrieval.
variants: nuanced vocabulary for describing the ways in which llms contribute to the writing process

dimensions.gloss: Whether the disclosure statement or its associated metadata is provided in a structured, machine-parseable form.
dimensions.note: Close call: one concerns AI-authorship disclosure statements in papers, the other a dataset repository's landing page, but both ask whether the disclosure/metadata can be parsed by machines rather than only read by humans.

dimensions.gloss: How complete or detailed the provenance information attached to (meta)data in a repository is.
dimensions.note: Same underlying repository-assessment field reported with two different value scales (unclear/adequate/full vs. no/yes).

dimensions.gloss: Whether a persistent researcher identifier (ORCID) can be, or is, linked to the record.
The maturity stage of the item being described, such as proposed, implemented, or evaluated.
Which specific provenance or attestation mechanism (watermark, digital signature, metadata tag, identity/payment attestation) is mentioned or used.
dimensions.note: Close call: 'mechanisms' lists technical content-provenance mechanisms (watermarks, signatures, tagging) while the attestation label comes from a separate identity/commerce attestation taxonomy, but both name the type of verification mechanism used.

dimensions.gloss: Whether, and what, consequences or penalties apply for failing to disclose AI use or content.
Whether the AI-use policy is presented as fixed or as subject to ongoing revision and adaptation.
Whether and how patients or the public were involved in designing, conducting, or co-developing the work.
How clearly the study population, eligibility criteria, and setting are specified.
The medium or format — interactive vs. static, or media type — in which disclosed information is presented.
What category of public trace an accountability disclosure takes, such as narrative disclosure or market information.
Whether the reporting is neutral and independent of the author's own opinions or biases.
What specific type of task or contribution a human contributor performed, as in a CRediT-style taxonomy.
The ordinal level or grade of a contributor's involvement, such as lead/equal/supporting.
Which category of AI technology (LLMs generally, ChatGPT specifically, other GAI tools) a piece of guidance addresses.
The chain of parties (developer, vendor, institution, practitioner) across whom liability or responsibility is distributed.
Whether a lighter or more minimal disclosure is appropriate given the low-impact nature of the AI use.
Whether and how the limitations of an AI-produced output are communicated to its audience.
Whether AI assistance expands or narrows the user's own communicative capacity.
Whether mandatory disclosure is framed as pedagogical metadata for learning versus mere compliance.
variants: mandatory disclosure as pedagogical metadata rather than merely as compliance

dimensions.gloss: Which stage of the manuscript's intellectual content — arguments, conclusions, methods, interpretation, or presentation — AI influenced.
How a study or report is mapped to the appropriate existing reporting guideline (e.g., CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI).
Whether and where the study's materials were reported as available.
Whether a scheme or policy mentions a mechanism for resolving disputes.
The formality/quality of qualified references to other (meta)data included in a repository's records.
Whether prompts are treated as methodological traces that shape a paper's claims, typologies, or interpretive frames.
How faculty enforce policies on AI misuse and integrity, including use of AI-detection software.
Whether widespread LLM integration is flagged as creating systemic vulnerability or dependency risk.
Which modality of honorary (undeserved) authorship is being described — gift, guest, or coercive.
Whether an output can be traced back to specific internal model components, such as neuron circuits or attention heads.
Which of several complementary modes of formally referencing a resource (citation, data citation, mention) is used.
Whether a governance system spanning multiple stakeholder groups (developers, regulators, civil society, users) is called for.
The name by which the research data used is identified.
The governance tier at which an AI-use policy sits, from national regulation down to course-specific guidance.
The nature of the evidence underlying a document, categorised as research, opinion, strategy documents, or raw data.
The new checklist items a reporting guideline adds specifically to describe an AI intervention (e.g., instructions, setting, input/output handling, human-AI interaction, error analysis).
The prevention of harm and risk to patients associated with generative AI use in healthcare.
Whether the disclosure establishes the exact governed object and representation the provenance claim applies to.
A named practice of pausing briefly during refinement to counteract the illusion of fluency from AI output.
How an AI-related artifact is classified in kind, e.g. as a digital scientific artefact.
Whether the study itself was published as open access.
The type of operation performed within an AI-mediated instructional arrangement.
A composite set of operational metrics (attribution integrity, intervention latency, cross-service traceability, adversarial robustness) used to assess AI governability.
The runtime dependencies, execution assumptions, access requirements, and cost/energy implications of running the AI system.
Operational risk as one named domain within a broader structured risk framework.
Provenance framed as an economic option value, via concepts like provenance capital, provenance debt, and remixability.
The value placed on individual initiative, discretion, and human authorship of academic work.
The follow-up time window and linkage rules (e.g., 6h/24h/30-day, censoring, competing events) used to track an outcome.
Whether primary/secondary outcomes and performance metrics were specified in advance of the study.
Whether and how AI outputs were reviewed, describing what was accepted, modified, rejected, or incorporated.
A composite vulnerability rating (moderate/high/very high) produced by a structured rubric.
Whether ownership and ownership history of a digital asset are encoded and referenced (e.g., via an NFT).
An enforcement layer that rejects malformed or forged provenance manifests on high-risk content, with rationale and appeal.
How a regulation defines the scope of what counts as AI-generated content requiring disclosure — unqualified, quantitatively qualified, qualitatively qualified, or undefined.
Whether a regulation's disclosure requirement applies generally, to specific use cases, or carries exceptions.
The page locator recorded alongside author/year/functional-role metadata for a coded source unit.
Participant interaction as one named theme among the research team, study design, data practices, and data analysis themes of a review framework.
Which production pathway (e.g., open-source vs. closed-source tooling, stepwise vs. enhanced generation) was used to create AI-generated media.
The alignment between AI-supported instructional processes and empirically grounded learning principles.
The perceived consequences that, alongside creative contribution and output involvement, drive where a disclosure threshold is set.
Whether a task's perceived risk in an AI-delegation framework is rated high or low.
A named phase (e.g., set an AI-free zone, struggle, spar with AI) in a structured framework for maintaining human cognitive skill alongside AI use.
Whether plagiarism screening is used as part of the integrity-checking process.
The maintainers' policies for erratum handling, updates, and deprecation of repository entries.
Whether a policy exists governing how changes to an authorship list are made.
variants: policies around making changes to authorship

dimensions.gloss: How the people subject to an AI-use policy interpret or rationalise it for themselves.
Which limited or vulnerable populations (e.g., neurodivergent, gender-diverse, non-Western, paediatric) a disclosure requirement's scope covers or excludes.
Ongoing evaluation of an AI system after deployment, framed as a component of a transparency regime.
